claims.claim: All overexpression lines of 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 showed a reduction in rosette area.
claims.source: All overexpression lines showed a reduction in rosette area (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Leaves of 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 plants appeared to be rounder than those of Col-0.
claims.source: In addition, leaves appeared to be rounder than those of Col-0, a phenotype that can also be observed in da1-1 plants, and the petioles were found to be shorter.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic observations and leaf blade index measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The petioles of 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 plants were found to be shorter than those of Col-0.
claims.source: In addition, leaves appeared to be rounder than those of Col-0, a phenotype that can also be observed in da1-1 plants, and the petioles were found to be shorter.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic observations.

claims.claim: da1-1 mutants have a significantly lower leaf blade index compared to Col-0.
claims.source: We could observe a significantly lower leaf blade index in da1-1 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and in two independent 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 lines compared to Col-0 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), meaning the leaves had a rounder shape.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by leaf blade index measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Two independent 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 lines have a significantly lower leaf blade index compared to Col-0.
claims.source: We could observe a significantly lower leaf blade index in da1-1 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and in two independent 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 lines compared to Col-0 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), meaning the leaves had a rounder shape.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by leaf blade index measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Homozygous plants of several 35S::UBP13 lines were stunted in growth and failed to produce a flower stalk and seeds.
claims.source: For several 35S::UBP13 lines, we were unable to produce stable seed stocks because the homozygous plants were stunted in growth (Figure 2A) and failed to produce a flower stalk and seeds.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic observations shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The ubp12-2 mutant showed a decrease in leaf area.
claims.source: After leaf area measurements, we could observe a decrease in leaf area in the ubp12-2 mutants (Figure 2B), in which the levels of both UBP12 and UBP13 transcripts were previously shown to be downregulated (Cui et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by leaf area measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: In ubp12-2 mutants, the levels of both UBP12 and UBP13 transcripts are downregulated.
claims.source: After leaf area measurements, we could observe a decrease in leaf area in the ubp12-2 mutants (Figure 2B), in which the levels of both UBP12 and UBP13 transcripts were previously shown to be downregulated (Cui et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cui et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Mutant lines in which only the expression of either UBP12 or UBP13 was downregulated displayed no differences in leaf size compared to the control.
claims.source: Mutant lines in which only the expression of either UBP12 or UBP13 was downregulated, displayed no differences in leaf size compared to the control (Figure 2—figure supplements 4–7).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by leaf area measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 4–7.

claims.claim: In all UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines, the significant decrease in leaf area was caused by a strong reduction in cell area.
claims.source: In all overexpression lines, the significant decrease in leaf area (29%, 26%, 33% and 36% for 35S::UBP12_3.1, 35S::UBP12_3.2, 35S::UBP13_1.1 and 35S::UBP13_2.3, respectively) was caused by a strong reduction in cell area (26%, 40%, 24% and 46% for 35S::UBP12_3.1, 35S::UBP12_3.2, 35S::UBP13_1.1 and 35S::UBP13_2.3, respectively), whereas the decrease in ubp12-2 leaf size (32%) resulted from a reduction in cell area (21%) and cell number (11%) (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cellular analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The decrease in ubp12-2 leaf size resulted from a reduction in cell area and cell number.
claims.source: In all overexpression lines, the significant decrease in leaf area (29%, 26%, 33% and 36% for 35S::UBP12_3.1, 35S::UBP12_3.2, 35S::UBP13_1.1 and 35S::UBP13_2.3, respectively) was caused by a strong reduction in cell area (26%, 40%, 24% and 46% for 35S::UBP12_3.1, 35S::UBP12_3.2, 35S::UBP13_1.1 and 35S::UBP13_2.3, respectively), whereas the decrease in ubp12-2 leaf size (32%) resulted from a reduction in cell area (21%) and cell number (11%) (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cellular analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines harbored a larger proportion of very small cells in addition to a general decrease in mature pavement cell size.
claims.source: A cell area distribution plot confirmed that indeed all independent UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines harbored a larger proportion of these small cells in addition to a general decrease in mature pavement cell size (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell area distribution data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: For the ubp12-2 mutant, no differences in cell area distribution compared to Col-0 could be observed.
claims.source: For the ubp12-2 mutant, no differences in cell area distribution compared to Col-0 could be observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 10).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell area distribution data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 10.

claims.claim: At nine days after stratification (DAS), all leaf cells of Col-0, 35S::UBP12_3.1 and 35S::UBP13_1.1 exhibited a 2C or 4C content, demonstrating the majority of cells are still in the mitotic cell cycle.
claims.source: At nine days after stratification (DAS), all leaf cells of the three lines exhibited a 2C or 4C content, demonstrating the majority of cells are still in the mitotic cell cycle (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: From 12 DAS onwards, cells with 8C started to appear, indicating the onset of endoreduplication.
claims.source: From 12 DAS onwards, cells with 8C started to appear, indicating the onset of endoreduplication.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: At 12 DAS, leaves of 35S::UBP12 plants contained a significantly larger proportion of 2C cells (53%) than those of the Col-0 (43%) and a significantly lower amount of 4C cells (44% and 52%, respectively).
claims.source: At 12 DAS, leaves of 35S::UBP12 plants contained a significantly larger proportion of 2 C cells (53%) than those of the Col-0 (43%) and a significantly lower amount of 4 C cells (44% and 52%, respectively).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: At 15 DAS, the amount of 8C nuclei was significantly lower in 35S::UBP12 (28%) than in the control (35%).
claims.source: At 15 DAS, the amount of 8C nuclei was significantly lower in 35S::UBP12 (28%) than in the control (35%) (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: 35S::UBP13 leaves had a significantly higher amount of 2C cells at 12 DAS (61%) and 15 DAS (42%) compared to Col-0 (43% and 25%, respectively).
claims.source: Similar, but more pronounced observations were found in 35S::UBP13 leaves, in which a significantly higher amount of 2 C cells was detected at 12 DAS (61%) and 15 DAS (42%) compared to Col-0 (43% and 25%, respectively).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: 35S::UBP13 leaves had a lower level of 4C cells at 12 DAS (35%) compared to Col-0 (52%).
claims.source: In addition, a lower level of 4 C cells was found at 12 DAS (35% in 35S::UBP13, 52% in Col-0) and fewer cells with 8C were present at 15, 18, 21 and 27 DAS in 35S::UBP13 (22%, 33%, 35% and 35%, respectively) compared to Col-0 (35%, 42%, 42% and 46%, respectively) (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Fewer cells with 8C were present at 15, 18, 21 and 27 DAS in 35S::UBP13 (22%, 33%, 35% and 35%, respectively) compared to Col-0 (35%, 42%, 42% and 46%, respectively).
claims.source: In addition, a lower level of 4 C cells was found at 12 DAS (35% in 35S::UBP13, 52% in Col-0) and fewer cells with 8C were present at 15, 18, 21 and 27 DAS in 35S::UBP13 (22%, 33%, 35% and 35%, respectively) compared to Col-0 (35%, 42%, 42% and 46%, respectively) (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: At 9 DAS, there was a significantly higher expression of ANT, GRF5 and KLUH in 35S::UBP13 lines compared to the Col-0.
claims.source: At 9 DAS, when all epidermal cells are actively dividing (Andriankaja et al., 2012), we could observe a significantly higher expression of ANT, GRF5 and KLUH in 35S::UBP13 lines compared to the Col-0 (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: At 12 DAS, there was a significant higher expression of AN3 and GRF5 and the cell division marker CYCB1;1 in 35S::UBP13 leaves.
claims.source: Later in development at 12 DAS, a large portion of the Col-0 cells should have exited the mitotic division cycle and start to differentiate (Andriankaja et al., 2012; Donnelly et al., 1999; Kazama et al., 2010). Still, there was a significant higher expression of AN3 and GRF5 and the cell division marker CYCB1;1 in 35S::UBP13 leaves (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: On 15 DAS, the expression levels of ANT and CYCB1;1 were elevated in 35S::UBP13 leaves.
claims.source: On 15 DAS, the expression levels of ANT and CYCB1;one were elevated in 35S::UBP13 leaves (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and finally, at 18 DAS, ANT was still significantly higher expressed in 35S::UBP13 compared to the Col-0 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: At 18 DAS, ANT was still significantly higher expressed in 35S::UBP13 compared to the Col-0.
claims.source: On 15 DAS, the expression levels of ANT and CYCB1;one were elevated in 35S::UBP13 leaves (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and finally, at 18 DAS, ANT was still significantly higher expressed in 35S::UBP13 compared to the Col-0 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: In Col-0 leaf tips at 12 DAS, the epidermal cells had started to expand and differentiate.
claims.source: To further explore these observations, we characterized the epidermal cells of tips of the third leaf of 12 day old seedlings, which should be undergoing cell differentiation at this stage in Col-0 (Andriankaja et al., 2012). In Col-0 leaf tips, we could indeed observe that the epidermal cells had started to expand and differentiate (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cellular imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Similar leaf tips of 35S::UBP12 or 35S::UBP13 plants at 12 DAS contained almost exclusively undifferentiated cells.
claims.source: On the contrary, similar leaf tips of 35S::UBP12 or 35S::UBP13 plants contained almost exclusively undifferentiated cells (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cellular imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Cell number was not significantly altered in UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines.
claims.source: These results, together with our observation that cell number was not significantly altered in UBP12 an UBP13 overexpression lines, indicate that especially during the early developmental stages of leaf growth, endoreduplication and cell differentiation are delayed in 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 leaves.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cellular analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Endoreduplication and cell differentiation are delayed in 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 leaves during the early developmental stages of leaf growth.
claims.source: These results, together with our observation that cell number was not significantly altered in UBP12 an UBP13 overexpression lines, indicate that especially during the early developmental stages of leaf growth, endoreduplication and cell differentiation are delayed in 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 leaves.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including ploidy analysis, gene expression data, and cellular imaging.

claims.claim: Ubiquitinated HIS-MBP-DA1 can be deubiquitinated by GST-UBP12 or GST-UBP13, but their respective catalytic mutants fail to do so.
claims.source: Figure 4A shows that ubiquitinated HIS-MBP-DA1 can be deubiquitinated by GST-UBP12 or GST-UBP13, but their respective catalytic mutants fail to do so.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro deubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Similar deubiquitination activities could be observed for the substrates DAR1 and DAR2.
claims.source: Similar deubiquitination activities could be observed for the substrates DAR1 and DAR2 (Figure 4B–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro deubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claims.claim: Both GST-UBP12 and GST-UBP13 could strongly deubiquitinate HIS-MBP-DA1, but no such effect could be observed upon addition of GST-UBP3, GST-UBP15 or GST-UBP24.
claims.source: We found again that both GST-UBP12 and GST-UBP13 could strongly deubiquitinate HIS-MBP-DA1, but no such effect could be observed upon addition of GST-UBP3, GST-UBP15 or GST-UBP24 (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro deubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: After 1 hr, a shift in molecular weight occurred in the ubiquitinated HIS-MBP-DA1 samples that were incubated with Col-0 extract, and this shift did not occur in the sample that was incubated with the ubp12-2 extract.
claims.source: Already after 1 hr, we could observe a shift in molecular weight in the ubiquitinated HIS-MBP-DA1 samples that were incubated with Col-0 extract (Figure 5A), and this shift did not occur in the sample that was incubated with the ubp12-2 extract (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell-free deubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claims.claim: The intensity of ubiquitinated HIS-MBP-DA1 bands faded faster in the presence of Col-0 extract than in the presence of ubp12-2 extract.
claims.source: In addition, the intensity of ubiquitinated HIS-MBP-DA1 bands faded faster in the presence of Col-0 extract than in the presence of ubp12-2 extract (Figure 5A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell-free deubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claims.claim: When ubiquitinated DA1 proteins were incubated with equal extracts of 35S::UBP12 or 35S::UBP13 plants, the intensity of ubiquitinated HIS-MBP-DA1 disappeared at a faster rate.
claims.source: In addition, when ubiquitinated DA1 proteins were incubated with equal extracts of 35S::UBP12 (Figure 5F) or 35S::UBP13 (Figure 5G) plants, the intensity of ubiquitinated HIS-MBP-DA1 disappeared at a faster rate (Figure 5D–H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell-free deubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 5D-H.

claims.claim: No increases in protein abundance were identified in the 35S::GFP-DA1_35S::UBP12 and 35S::GFP-DA1_35S::UBP13 samples compared to those of 35S::GFP-DA1.
claims.source: In addition, we extracted proteins of 35S::GFP-DA1, 35S::GFP-DA1_35S::UBP12 and 35S::GFP-DA1_35S::UBP13 plants and performed a purification with anti-GFP beads from equal protein inputs. After purification, we submitted the samples to Western Blot and detected the abundance of GFP-DA1 proteins. We could not identify increases in protein abundance in the 35S::GFP-DA1_35S::UBP12 and 35S::GFP-DA1_35S::UBP13 samples compared to those of 35S::GFP-DA1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting UBP12 and UBP13 do not prevent potential removal of polyubiquitination of DA1 and hereby prevent its degradation by the proteasome.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: UBP12 and UBP13 do not prevent potential removal of polyubiquitination of DA1 and hereby prevent its degradation by the proteasome.
claims.source: We could not identify increases in protein abundance in the 35S::GFP-DA1_35S::UBP12 and 35S::GFP-DA1_35S::UBP13 samples compared to those of 35S::GFP-DA1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting UBP12 and UBP13 do not prevent potential removal of polyubiquitination of DA1 and hereby prevent its degradation by the proteasome.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: After 4 hr of incubation, the intensities of all GST-tagged UBP proteins were equal and no additional cleaving fragments could be observed in the HIS-MBP-DA1 samples compared to those with HIS-MBP-DA1H418A,H422A.
claims.source: However, after 4 hr of incubation, the intensities of all GST-tagged UBP proteins were equal and no additional cleaving fragments could be observed in the HIS-MBP-DA1 samples compared to those with HIS-MBP-DA1H418A,H422A (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro cleaving assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: In all double overexpression lines of 35S::GFP-DA1 and 35S::UBP12 or 35S::UBP13, similar phenotypes as in the 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 lines in the Col-0 background were observed.
claims.source: In all double overexpression lines, we could observe similar phenotypes as in the 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 lines in the Col-0 background (Figure 6B, Figure 2A), suggesting that the UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression phenotype is dominant and UBP12 and UBP13 are not destabilized by DA1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression phenotype is dominant.
claims.source: In all double overexpression lines, we could observe similar phenotypes as in the 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 lines in the Col-0 background (Figure 6B, Figure 2A), suggesting that the UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression phenotype is dominant and UBP12 and UBP13 are not destabilized by DA1.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from genetic analysis of double overexpression lines.

claims.claim: UBP12 and UBP13 are not destabilized by DA1.
claims.source: In all double overexpression lines, we could observe similar phenotypes as in the 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 lines in the Col-0 background (Figure 6B, Figure 2A), suggesting that the UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression phenotype is dominant and UBP12 and UBP13 are not destabilized by DA1.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from genetic analysis of double overexpression lines.

claims.claim: UBP12 and UBP13 act upstream of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 to counteract their ubiquitination.
claims.source: Thus, our biochemical, genetic and phenotypic analyses show that UBP12 and UBP13 are not cleavage substrates, but act upstream of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 to counteract their ubiquitination.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including deubiquitination assays, cleaving assays, and genetic analyses.

claims.claim: By limiting their peptidase activity, UBP12 and UBP13 fine-tune leaf growth, cell size and endoreduplication.
claims.source: By limiting their peptidase activity, UBP12 and UBP13 fine-tune leaf growth, cell size and endoreduplication.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including phenotypic, cellular, and molecular analyses.

claims.claim: UBP12 and UBP13 work antagonistically to BB and DA2.
claims.source: In this study, we identified two ubiquitin-specific proteases, UBP12 an UBP13, that interact with DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 in vitro and in vivo. Our experiments demonstrate that these UBPs work antagonistically to BB and DA2.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from deubiquitination assays and genetic analyses.

claims.claim: Incubation of ubiquitinated DA1, DAR1 or DAR2 with either UBP12 or UBP13 resulted in strong deubiquitination.
claims.source: Incubation of ubiquitinated DA1, DAR1 or DAR2 with either UBP12 or UBP13 resulted in strong deubiquitination.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro deubiquitination assays shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: UBP12 and UBP13 can also interact with the unubiquitinated forms of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2.
claims.source: Interestingly, our in vitro immunoprecipitation (IP) shows that UBP12 and UBP13 can also interact with the unubiquitinated forms of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro pull-down data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claims.claim: UBP15 has no deubiquitination activity towards DA1.
claims.source: Our results indicate that UBP15 has no deubiquitination activity towards DA1 and acts therefore downstream in this pathway.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro deubiquitination assays shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: UBP15 acts downstream in the DA1 pathway.
claims.source: Our results indicate that UBP15 has no deubiquitination activity towards DA1 and acts therefore downstream in this pathway.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from deubiquitination assays and prior knowledge about UBP15 being a cleavage substrate of DA1.

claims.claim: UBP12 and UBP13 have recently been described to deubiquitinate various poly-ubiquitinated proteins, preventing their proteasomal degradation.
claims.source: UBP12 and UBP13 have recently been described to deubiquitinate various poly-ubiquitinated proteins, preventing their proteasomal degradation (An et al., 2018; Jeong et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2019; Park et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to An et al., 2018; Jeong et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2019; Park et al., 2019.

claims.claim: UBP12 and UBP13 can decrease the levels of mono-ubiquitinated H2A.
claims.source: In addition, they can decrease the levels of mono-ubiquitinated H2A (Derkacheva et al., 2016) and remove multiple mono-ubiquitinations from DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 as described here.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Derkacheva et al., 2016.

claims.claim: UBP12 and UBP13 remove multiple mono-ubiquitinations from DA1, DAR1 and DAR2.
claims.source: In addition, they can decrease the levels of mono-ubiquitinated H2A (Derkacheva et al., 2016) and remove multiple mono-ubiquitinations from DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 as described here.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro deubiquitination assays shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: UBP12 and UBP13 demonstrate flexibility towards different types of ubiquitination.
claims.source: This demonstrates the flexibility of these UBPs towards different types of ubiquitination (Clague et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that UBP12 and UBP13 can deubiquitinate both poly-ubiquitinated proteins and multiple mono-ubiquitinated proteins.

claims.claim: No evidence was found that besides the removal of the multiple mono-ubiquitination sites of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2, potential degradation of these proteins by removal of poly-ubiquitination was mediated by UBP12 or UBP13.
claims.source: Here, we could not find evidence that besides the removal of the multiple mono-ubiquitination sites of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2, potential degradation of these proteins by removal of poly-ubiquitination was mediated by UBP12 or UBP13.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Downregulation of either UBP12 or UBP13 did not alter leaf size, indicating that these genes work redundantly in controlling leaf size.
claims.source: In contrast to the early flowering time-related genes (Cui et al., 2013), downregulation of either UBP12 or UBP13 did not alter leaf size, indicating that these genes work redundantly in controlling leaf size.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by leaf area measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 4–7.

claims.claim: The leaf area was only reduced in ubp12-2 mutants, in which levels of both UBP12 and UBP13 are decreased.
claims.source: The leaf area was only reduced in ubp12-2 mutants, in which levels of both UBP12 and UBP13 are decreased (Cui et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by leaf area measurements shown in Figure 2B and a citation to Cui et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The decreased deubiquitination activity towards DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 could result in an accumulation of the activated peptidases in ubp12-2 mutants, leading to a decrease in cell number and leaf area.
claims.source: The subsequently decreased deubiquitination activity towards DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 could result in an accumulation of the activated peptidases in ubp12-2 mutants, leading to a decrease in cell number and leaf area.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the phenotypic data.

claims.claim: A similar phenotype to ubp12-2 is also observed in GFP-DA1 overexpressing plants and in the ubp15 mutant.
claims.source: A similar phenotype is also observed in GFP-DA1 overexpressing plants (Vanhaeren et al., 2017) and in the ubp15 mutant (Du et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vanhaeren et al., 2017; Du et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2008.

claims.claim: High ectopic expression of either UBP12 or UBP13 would result in very low levels of ubiquitinated DA1, DAR1 and DAR2, leading to a severe disturbance of leaf development.
claims.source: In contrast, high ectopic expression of either UBP12 or UBP13 would result in very low levels of ubiquitinated DA1, DAR1 and DAR2, leading to a severe disturbance of leaf development.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the phenotypic data.

claims.claim: 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 plants were strongly reduced in growth in a similar manner as da1ko_dar1-1_dar2-1 triple mutants.
claims.source: Indeed, 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 plants were strongly reduced in growth in a similar manner as da1ko_dar1-1_dar2-1 triple mutants (Peng et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figure 2A and a citation to Peng et al., 2015.

claims.claim: A more detailed cellular and molecular analysis of 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 leaves revealed a strong reduction in cell area and a decrease in ploidy levels at the early stages of leaf development, which were also observed in da1ko_dar1-1_dar2-1 plants.
claims.source: A more detailed cellular and molecular analysis of 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 leaves revealed more parallels, such as a strong reduction in cell area and a decrease in ploidy levels at the early stages of leaf development, which were also observed in da1ko_dar1-1_dar2-1 plants (Peng et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cellular and ploidy data shown in Figures 2 and 3, and a citation to Peng et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The complete absence of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 proteins in da1ko_dar1-1_dar2-1 plants could explain its stronger reduction in endoreduplication than that of UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines.
claims.source: The complete absence of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 proteins in da1ko_dar1-1_dar2-1 plants could however explain its stronger reduction in endoreduplication than that of UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines, in which ubiquitination of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 can still occur, but is likely kept at a very low level.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation comparing the phenotypes of different genotypes.

claims.claim: Several markers of cell proliferation were found to be more highly expressed in 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 during early stages of leaf development, similarly as observed in plants that contain a DA1R358K mutation.
claims.source: In addition, several markers of cell proliferation were found to be more highly expressed in 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 during early stages of leaf development, similarly as observed in plants that contain a DA1R358K mutation (Vanhaeren et al., 2017), which reduces the peptidase activity of DA1 (Dong et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3B-C and citations to Vanhaeren et al., 2017 and Dong et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The final cell number in the UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines was not increased, suggesting that a strong reduction of DA1 activity rather delays development but does not increase the duration of cell proliferation and hence the final number of cells.
claims.source: However, the final cell number in the UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines was not increased, suggesting that a strong reduction of DA1 activity rather delays development but does not increase the duration of cell proliferation and hence the final number of cells.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from cellular analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 negatively regulate their own activity by cleaving their activating E3-ligases BB and DA2, resulting in an activation-repression system.
claims.source: Previously, it has been shown that DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 negatively regulate their own activity by cleaving their activating E3-ligases BB and DA2, resulting in an activation-repression system (Dong et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dong et al., 2017.

claims.claim: UBP12 and UBP13 form an additional layer of post-translational regulation to limit the activity of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 by specifically removing ubiquitin.
claims.source: UBP12 and UBP13 form an additional layer of post-translational regulation to limit the activity of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 by specifically removing ubiquitin, and hence further fine-tune organ growth in this growth-regulatory pathway.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claims.claim: This dual system to limit and fine-tune the activity of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 demonstrates the importance of keeping a correct balance between the active and inactive pool of these proteases during leaf development.
claims.source: This dual system to limit and fine-tune the activity of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 demonstrates the importance of keeping a correct balance between the active and inactive pool of these proteases during leaf development.
claims.evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claims.claim: In wild-type conditions, a correct balance between an inactive and active (ubiquitinated) DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 results in an intact exit from mitosis and standard ploidy levels in leaf cells, which leads to normal plant growth.
claims.source: In wild-type conditions, a correct balance between an inactive and active (ubiquitinated) DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 results in an intact exit from mitosis and standard ploidy levels in leaf cells, which leads to normal plant growth (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is a model summarizing the findings, illustrated in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: High levels of UBP12 or UBP13 can shift the balance to a depletion of activated DA1, DAR1 and DAR2, which results in a delayed endoreduplication, a severe reduction in cell size and stunted plant growth.
claims.source: High levels of UBP12 or UBP13 can however shift the balance to a depletion of activated DA1, DAR1 and DAR2, which results in a delayed endoreduplication, a severe reduction in cell size and stunted plant growth (Figure 7B), which is highly similar to the phenotype of da1ko_dar1-1_dar2-1 mutants (Peng et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a model summarizing the findings, illustrated in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Low levels of UBP12 and UBP13 might lead to an increase in activated DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 levels, more destabilization of its substrates and can hence limit plant growth by reducing both cell area and cell number.
claims.source: Low levels of UBP12 and UBP13 might on the other hand lead to an increase in activated DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 levels, more destabilization of its substrates and can hence limit plant growth by reducing both cell area and cell number (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is a model summarizing the findings, illustrated in Figure 7C.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Peng et al., 2015 and Vanhaeren et al., 2017.

claims.claim: It remains unclear if the reduction in cell area in the ubp12-2 mutants or UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines results only from altered levels of DA1 activity, or if UBP12 and UBP13 regulate cell expansion through other growth regulators.
claims.source: Additionally, it remains also unclear if this reduction in cell area in the ubp12-2 mutants or UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines results only from altered levels of DA1 activity, or if UBP12 and UBP13 regulate cell expansion through other growth regulators.
claims.evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the study.

results.result: UBP12 and UBP13 physically interact with DA1, DAR1, and DAR2 in vivo and in vitro, and these proteins are co-expressed and co-localize during leaf development.
results.evaluation: Claims C24, C40-C43 provide converging evidence from multiple independent methods (IP-MS/MS, in vitro pull-down, in vivo pull-down, confocal microscopy) demonstrating physical interaction. Claims C44-C47 establish co-expression and co-localization patterns consistent with functional interaction. The use of multiple orthogonal approaches and appropriate controls (free GST, free GFP) strengthens confidence in this result.

results.result: UBP12 and UBP13 deubiquitinate DA1, DAR1, and DAR2 in vitro, removing multiple mono-ubiquitinations and reducing their peptidase activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C37, C77-C79, C92, and C98 are supported by in vitro deubiquitination assays (Figure 4) showing that wild-type UBP12/13 remove ubiquitin from DA1/DAR1/DAR2, while catalytic mutants do not. The specificity is demonstrated by testing other UBPs (UBP3, UBP15, UBP24) that lack this activity (C79). The experimental design includes appropriate negative controls (catalytic mutants, other UBPs).

results.result: Cell-free extracts from plants with different UBP12/UBP13 levels show differential deubiquitination activity toward DA1, with higher activity in Col-0 compared to ubp12-2 mutants and enhanced activity in overexpression lines.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 are supported by cell-free deubiquitination assays (Figure 5A-H) showing dose-dependent effects of UBP12/13 levels on DA1 deubiquitination. The use of equal protein inputs and time-course measurements strengthens the quantitative interpretation. However, the manuscript notes that later time points (6-8 hr) could not be interpreted due to background issues, which is appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: UBP12 and UBP13 are not cleavage substrates of activated DA1, DAR1, or DAR2, and the UBP12/13 overexpression phenotype is dominant over DA1 overexpression.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C38, and C85 are supported by in vitro cleaving assays (Figure 6A) showing no cleavage of UBP12/13 by active DA1 after 4 hr incubation. Claims C86-C88 are supported by genetic analysis of double overexpression lines (Figure 6B) showing that UBP12/13 overexpression phenotypes persist in the presence of DA1 overexpression. This epistasis analysis supports the upstream positioning of UBP12/13 in the pathway.

results.result: Overexpression of UBP12 or UBP13 strongly decreases leaf size and cell area, with leaves appearing rounder and having shorter petioles.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C48-C53, and C57 are supported by phenotypic measurements (Figure 2A-C) showing significant reductions in rosette area (26-36%), cell area (24-46%), and leaf blade index in multiple independent overexpression lines. The use of multiple independent transgenic lines and quantitative measurements of both organ and cellular phenotypes provides robust support. Some homozygous UBP13 lines were severely stunted and sterile (C53), indicating strong phenotypic effects.

results.result: The ubp12-2 mutant, in which both UBP12 and UBP13 are downregulated, produces smaller leaves with reduced cell area and cell number, while single mutants show no leaf size phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C54, C55, C56, C58, C101, and C102 are supported by phenotypic analysis (Figure 2B-C, Figure 2—figure supplements 4-7) showing that ubp12-2 has reduced leaf area (32%) due to decreases in both cell area (21%) and cell number (11%), while single UBP12 or UBP13 mutants show no phenotype. This demonstrates functional redundancy between UBP12 and UBP13 in controlling leaf size, consistent with prior work (C55, citing Cui et al., 2013).

results.result: Overexpression of UBP12 or UBP13 results in lower ploidy levels and delayed onset of endoreduplication during leaf development.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C61-C67 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 3A) showing time-course analysis of ploidy levels from 9-27 DAS. The data show significantly higher proportions of 2C cells and lower proportions of 8C cells in UBP12/13 overexpression lines compared to Col-0 at multiple time points, with effects more pronounced in 35S::UBP13. The use of multiple time points and statistical testing (indicated by significance markers) supports the conclusion of delayed endoreduplication.

results.result: Overexpression of UBP12 or UBP13 delays cell differentiation and maintains higher expression of cell proliferation markers during early leaf development.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C76 are supported by gene expression analysis (Figure 3B-C, Figure 3—figure supplements 3-4) and cellular imaging (Figure 3D) showing elevated expression of proliferation markers (ANT, GRF5, KLUH, CYCB1;1) at multiple developmental stages and persistence of undifferentiated cells at 12 DAS in UBP12/13 overexpression lines. The integration of molecular and cellular data provides strong support for delayed differentiation, though the mechanistic link to DA1/DAR1/DAR2 activity requires further validation.

results.result: UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines harbor a larger proportion of very small cells in addition to a general decrease in mature pavement cell size, while ubp12-2 shows no difference in cell area distribution.
results.evaluation: Claims C59 and C60 are supported by cell area distribution analysis (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 10) showing a shift toward smaller cell sizes in overexpression lines but not in ubp12-2 mutants. This suggests that high UBP12/13 levels may affect cell expansion dynamics differently than loss of function, though the biological significance of this bimodal distribution is not fully explained.

results.result: UBP12 and UBP13 do not prevent degradation of DA1 by removing polyubiquitination chains.
results.evaluation: Claims C83, C84, and C100 are supported by Western blot analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) showing no increase in GFP-DA1 protein abundance in double overexpression lines with UBP12 or UBP13. This negative result appropriately distinguishes the mechanism of UBP12/13 (removing activating mono-ubiquitinations) from preventing proteasomal degradation (which would require removing poly-ubiquitin chains). The conclusion is appropriately cautious.

results.result: UBP12 and UBP13 work upstream of DA1, DAR1, and DAR2 to restrict their protease activity by deubiquitination, thereby fine-tuning plant growth and development.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C89, C90, C91, and C112 represent integrative conclusions drawn from multiple lines of evidence: (1) UBP12/13 deubiquitinate DA1/DAR1/DAR2 in vitro, (2) UBP12/13 are not cleaved by DA1/DAR1/DAR2, (3) UBP12/13 overexpression phenocopies loss of DA1/DAR1/DAR2 function, and (4) genetic epistasis shows UBP12/13 act upstream. These conclusions are well-supported by the collective experimental evidence, though direct demonstration that deubiquitination reduces peptidase activity in vivo would strengthen the mechanistic link.

results.result: UBP12 and UBP13 can interact with unubiquitinated forms of DA1, DAR1, and DAR2, while UBP15 has no deubiquitination activity toward DA1 and acts downstream in the pathway.
results.evaluation: Claim C93 is supported by in vitro pull-down data (Figure 1D-F) showing interaction with unubiquitinated proteins. Claims C94 and C95 are supported by deubiquitination assays (Figure 4D) showing UBP15 lacks activity toward DA1, combined with prior knowledge that UBP15 is a cleavage substrate of DA1. This appropriately positions UBP15 downstream and distinguishes it from UBP12/13.

results.result: UBP12/13 mutants and overexpression lines exhibit phenotypes overlapping with DA1 overexpression and da1ko_dar1-1_dar2-1 triple mutants, respectively, consistent with UBP12/13 regulating DA1/DAR1/DAR2 activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C39 and C103-C110 are supported by comparative phenotypic analysis (Figures 2-3) and citations to prior work on DA1/DAR1/DAR2 mutants and overexpression lines. The phenotypic similarities (reduced leaf size, cell area, ploidy levels, delayed differentiation) provide strong genetic evidence for UBP12/13 acting in the same pathway as DA1/DAR1/DAR2. The interpretation that ubp12-2 leads to accumulation of activated peptidases (C103) is mechanistically reasonable but indirect.

results.result: Background knowledge about ubiquitination in plants, DUB classification, UBP12/13 functions, and the DA1/DAR1/DAR2 pathway from prior literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C9-C23, C25-C36, C46, C96, C97, C99, C111, C117, and C118 represent established knowledge from prior literature, appropriately cited throughout the manuscript. These claims provide essential context for interpreting the current findings. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are consistent with the cited literature. No evaluation of new experimental data is required for these background claims.

results.result: A tight balance between active and inactive DA1, DAR1, and DAR2 is crucial for normal plant development, with UBP12/13 providing an additional regulatory layer to maintain this balance.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C116 and C118 represent a conceptual model (Figure 7) integrating the study's findings with prior knowledge. The model is well-supported by the experimental data showing that both high and low DA1 activity (achieved through manipulating UBP12/13 levels) result in growth defects. The model appropriately synthesizes the dual regulatory mechanisms (self-cleavage of BB/DA2 and deubiquitination by UBP12/13) that control DA1/DAR1/DAR2 activity.

results.result: Unknown post-translational modifications of UBP12/13 may regulate their activity, and it remains unclear whether UBP12/13 regulate cell expansion solely through DA1/DAR1/DAR2 or through other growth regulators.
results.evaluation: Claims C119 and C120 represent speculative statements and acknowledged limitations of the study. C119 is a reasonable hypothesis based on constant expression levels and knowledge of other DUBs, but lacks experimental support. C120 appropriately acknowledges that the study does not definitively establish whether UBP12/13 effects on cell area are solely mediated through DA1/DAR1/DAR2. These represent important areas for future investigation.
